articles.title: From hands to tools: evidence for evolutionary precursors of tool processing in macaque cortex.
articles.content: In humans, hands are animate effectors and tools are visually dissimilar inanimate objects, yet the brain represents them in closely related cortical systems. Whether this coupling depends uniquely on human tool knowledge or reflects a conserved property of primate cortex is unknown. Using whole brain fMRI (0.22 cubic mm voxels) in macaques viewing images of hands, tools, and other objects, we found that inferotemporal cortex largely followed the animate/inanimate division, with only a few small hand-tool preferring sites. In contrast, parietal and prefrontal areas showed hand-tool representational similarities that were best matched by a neural-network model trained on fine-grained human hand-object interactions rather than by networks optimized for static object recognition or general action recognition. Volumetric functional ultrasound imaging (0.0023 cubic mm voxels) independently showed that tool responses were spatially aligned with human hand, but not monkey hand, responses in posterior parietal cortex. Macaque cortex thus represents tools in relation to the hand even without habitual tool use, consistent with an evolutionarily conserved action related scaffold that may be shaped by longterm visual exposure to human hand tool interactions.

articles.title: Determinants of domain-specific cognitive impairment after stroke: a mega-analysis of 13 acute ischaemic stroke cohorts
articles.content: The relationship between brain lesions and cognition is enigmatic. Apparently similar lesions can produce different outcomes. Stroke provides a prototypical model to understand how lesion anatomy, network disruption, prior injury and patient characteristics shape impairment. We analysed 3,034 patients from 13 acute ischaemic stroke cohorts, integrating infarct size and location, structural and functional lesion network mapping, pre-existing cerebrovascular injury, and demographic and clinical characteristics to predict impairment across six cognitive domains within one year after stroke. Infarct topography and connectivity improved prediction for six of seven outcomes over demographic, clinical and infarct-size information alone. Structural lesion connectivity accounted for most gains, with additional gains from topography and connectivity of pre-existing vascular lesions. Across domains, gains rested on left anterior thalamic connectivity plus domain-specific anatomy. Our findings establish, at unprecedented scale, that understanding lesion-cognition relationships requires looking beyond the lesion to networks, prior brain pathology and individual context.

articles.title: Spectral power-laws emerge naturally from realistic tuning curve heterogeneity
articles.content: How the brain represents the outside world with precision and allows for generalization is a fundamental question in neuroscience. One way of interpreting activity in neural systems is by contrasting two opposing coding principles: efficient coding, which produces high-dimensional, uncorrelated representations that maximally differentiate stimuli, and robust coding, which produces low-dimensional, smooth representations that generalize across stimuli. The decay of the eigenspectrum of the covariance matrix provides an intuitive perspective on this trade-off and has previously been observed to follow a critical power-law in the brain. While tuning curve heterogeneity has been proposed as a potential mechanism from which these power-laws could emerge, it remains unclear how specific biological properties of tuning curve heterogeneity give rise to them and how the organization of this heterogeneity maps onto the broader computational trade-offs between generalization, capacity, and noise robustness. In this work, we theoretically link tuning curve heterogeneity to spectral power-laws and use this biologically grounded model to investigate how different representations affect generalization, noise robustness, precision, and capacity in a linear decoder. We show mathematically that a population of Gaussian tuning curves with Gamma-distributed widths and a power-law relationship between peak firing rate and tuning width — both properties reflected in data from hippocampal place fields and V1 orientation tuning — is sufficient to produce power-law eigenspectra. This model can be used to construct tuning curve populations on the continuum between the robust and efficient coding schemes. These findings provide a biologically realistic explanation of spectral power-laws in neural populations, demonstrate the importance of tuning curve population statistics for neural coding, and allow for estimating the spectral decay from tuning curve statistics alone, circumventing the large populations and extensive stimulus sets typically required to directly compute this for noisy neural responses.
articles.author: Federico Stella

articles.title: Neural correlates of executive functioning among adolescents and young adults living with HIV: a systematic review of structural and functional imaging studies
articles.content: IntroductionReduced executive functioning (EF) - including inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, and working memory - has been frequently observed among adolescents and young adults living with HIV (AYALH), despite antiretroviral therapy (ART). These deficits may reflect HIV-associated alterations in brain structure and function. This review aimed to synthesize the available evidence of this relationship.MethodsFollowing the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we searched PsycINFO, PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases for relevant studies reporting EF outcomes and neural correlates (structural or functional).ResultsTwenty studies met the inclusion criteria. Significantly lower brain volumes and cortical thickness, lower fractional anisotropy, higher mean diffusivity, higher cerebral blood flow, and altered cerebral metabolites were observed among AYALH relative to matched controls. EF problems, particularly in working memory, were frequently reported. Overall, the observed neural alterations correlated with decreased EF among AYALH.ConclusionDespite ART use, HIV-associated neural alterations and executive function deficits still occur or persist among adolescents and young adults living with HIV. Preliminary evidence suggests that distinct HIV-associated neural alterations may be associated with EF problems in AYALH. Neuroimaging may offer insights into these cognitive difficulties, although more longitudinal and multimodal studies are needed.Systematic Review RegistrationThis review is registered in PROSPERO (https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/), registration number: CRD42025639283.
articles.author: Amina Abubakar

articles.title: Cyborg dementia: could structural disembodiment accelerate brain aging via loss of muscle-bone trophic signaling? A matter of perspective
articles.content: Advances in brain-machine interfaces and neuroprosthetics are often framed as a path toward overcoming the biological limits of the body, with the eventual replacement of failing limbs and organs by durable artificial substitutes. Interestingly, this optimistic narrative overlooks a challenge that is becoming increasingly apparent in aging neuroscience: brain health depends critically on a continuous supply of trophic signals originating from skeletal muscle and bone. Myokines and osteokines such as irisin, uncarboxylated osteocalcin, and cathepsin B act on the brain to sustain BDNF expression, synaptic plasticity, and neurogenesis, forming what has been described as a muscle-bone-brain axis; disuse and immobilization, even in the absence of any primary brain pathology, are sufficient to disrupt this signaling and accelerate cognitive decline. This raises a largely unaddressed question for cyborg technologies: could a robotic body, mechanically capable of movement but biologically inert and secreting none of the trophic factors that living muscle and bone normally provide, deprive the brain of signals it needs to remain healthy, thereby accelerating, rather than preventing, neural aging? We term this hypothetical condition cyborg dementia. Rather than a purely engineering problem of motor control and sensory feedback, this reframes brain-machine interface design as fundamentally about preserving the endocrine dialogue between brain and musculoskeletal system, extending the goals of neuroprosthetics beyond restoring action to protecting the neuroendocrine mechanisms that biological embodiment was silently providing all along.
articles.author: Sungkun Chun

articles.title: AI and multiomics in stem cell-based repair after ischemic stroke: current evidence and validation priorities
articles.content: AI and multiomics can describe therapeutic cell and extracellular-vesicle (EV) products and the postischemic environment, but a molecular signature matters only if it changes a defined development or treatment decision. Existing reviews address stroke single-cell and spatial biology, AI in stem-cell multiomics, or AI-enabled regenerative engineering. This critical narrative review connects those topics through three decisions: whether a finished product has reproducible activity, which host conditions permit that activity, and whether a patient gains benefit attributable to treatment. We compare integration methods by their assumptions for paired, unpaired and mosaic data; distinguish Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation and universal cell embeddings by input encoding and learning objective; and examine why larger pretraining has not produced consistent gains over simpler baselines. A worked EV-potency task specifies candidate functional labels, independent training units, controls and external validation. Representative stroke studies are mapped from molecular description through experimentally tested mechanisms to prediction of unseen product lots and controlled clinical benefit. The reviewed stroke and adjacent cerebrovascular literature includes AI-assisted molecular prioritization, computational graft-host analysis and automated behavior quantification, but does not establish an externally validated AI predictor of finished-product potency or treatment-attributable patient benefit. Cross-scale virtual-cell and heterogeneous protein representations offer transferable methods, not validated ischemic-repair models. The framework identifies the experiments needed to turn molecular associations into decisions with measurable biological value.
articles.author: Chao Cheng

articles.title: Endothelial activation, neuronal injury, and blood–brain barrier dysfunction in postoperative acute kidney injury-associated delirium; a prospective observational study
articles.content: BackgroundDelirium occurs in up to 52% of cardiac and vascular surgeries and is associated with long-term cognitive impairment and death. Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a delirium risk factor. In rodents, AKI induces systemic endothelial activation and, when combined with surgery, results in greater neuroinflammation than surgery alone. We hypothesized that systemic endothelial activation and blood-brain barrier BBB disruption are more strongly associated with delirium that occurs concurrently with AKI.MethodsWe performed a prospective study of 150 adults undergoing cardiac and major vascular surgery. We quantified intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) and E-selectin, biomarkers of endothelial activation, and ubiquitin carboxy-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1), a biomarker of neuronal injury and BBB permeability, in plasma collected after surgery. Delirium was assessed using the CAM-ICU tool. KDIGO serum creatinine criteria were used to assess AKI.ResultsPatients with AKI-associated delirium and those with non-AKI-associated delirium had similar clinical characteristics, delirium risk factors, and postoperative sedation scores. In multivariable models, ICAM-1 was not associated with delirium overall (p = 0.29). However, AKI modified the association between ICAM-1 and postoperative delirium (p = 0.01 for interaction between AKI and ICAM-1) such that when the interaction term was introduced, the estimated ICAM-1 OR was 0.57 [95% CI 0.37–0.87], p = 0.01. In post-hoc analyses, higher ICAM-1 concentrations were associated with decreased odds of non-AKI-associated delirium (OR = 0.48 [95% CI 0.28–0.81], p = 0.01) and increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 1.69 [95% CI 1.05–2.74], p = 0.03). E-selectin was not associated with delirium. Higher UCHL1 concentrations were associated with an increased odds of AKI-associated delirium (OR = 3.68 [95% CI 2.05–6.62], p < 0.001), but not non-AKI-associated delirium (p = 0.33). This association between higher UCHL1 and a greater odds of AKI-associated delirium was potentiated by increased ICAM-1 endothelial activation (p = 0.046).ConclusionDelirium occurring concurrently with AKI may represent a biologically distinct phenotype. Recognition of biologic heterogeneity within delirium populations may help explain inconsistent associations reported for delirium risk factors and biomarkers. Accounting for this biological heterogeneity may improve the identification of delirium biomarkers and therapeutic targets and should be considered in future delirium research. Future multi-center studies with larger and more diverse cohorts and extended cognitive assessment protocols are needed to validate these observations.
articles.author: Loren E. Smith

articles.title: A hardware-aware open-source framework for design space exploration of mixed-signal spiking neural networks
articles.content: IntroductionEnergy-efficient neuromorphic computing at the edge requires simulation tools that can capture the non-ideal behavior of mixed-signal spiking neural network (SNN) hardware while supporting system-level design exploration.MethodsThis work presents an open-source hardware-aware simulation framework for mixed-signal SNNs that enables comparative analysis across neuron, synapse and architecture choices. The framework supports multiple neuron models, including Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF), Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) and Axon-Hillock (AH), together with non-volatile analog synapses based on floating-gate transistors and ReRAM devices. By incorporating device-level non-linearities directly into PyTorch-based training and inference, the tool enables optimization of physical synaptic parameters rather than idealized abstract weights.ResultsThe framework is evaluated on standard neuromorphic benchmarks, including N-MNIST, DVS Gesture and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD). For each model dataset configuration, it reports classification accuracy together with hardware-oriented metrics such as silicon area, power consumption and quantization sensitivity. In addition, mismatch analysis has been implemented to capture the impact of real silicon fabrication-based effects, such as device-to-device and transistor-level variability, on network behavior.DiscussionThese capabilities enable cross-layer design space exploration and help identify neuron-synapse configurations that best satisfy application-specific constraints on accuracy, energy efficiency, area and hardware fidelity.
articles.author: Sahil Shah

articles.title: Imaging fast neural circuit activity in brain and nerve with electrical impedance tomography (fnEIT): review, method and engineering aspects
articles.content: Fast neural electrical impedance tomography (fnEIT) is a technique for imaging neural activity in the brain or nerves, with a resolution of milliseconds and millimetres, using a probing applied current and boundary or depth voltage measurement. Proof of principle has been demonstrated in animal studies, but it is yet to be adopted into common use. Objective. The purpose of this review is to provide an introduction and overview of the method and technical aspects of fnEIT research and its place in the biomedical sciences. Topics covered include the bioimpedance of action potentials, fnEIT studies to date, similar EIT methods and technical innovations. Approach. A methodical critical review of the fnEIT literature has been performed. Promising areas of future work and their applications are highlighted, including challenges that must be overcome. Main results. It is shown that the fields of nerve imaging and neuromodulation, cognitive neuroscience in animals and humans, and epileptic seizure localisation could benefit from the ability of fnEIT to image millisecond scale neuronal depolarization throughout brain or nerve. This is achievable with existing methods but with current limitations of the need for implanted cranial or nerve electrodes and averaging to a repeated stimulus. Current approaches to overcome this include CMOS integrated active electrodes, frequency division multiplexing for parallel signal acquisition, and recording with atomic magnetometers. With these, it is a realistic possibility to achieve non-invasive imaging of fast neural activity in real-time with an electrode-atomic magnetometer helmet in human subjects with a resolution of mm and msec. Significance. This review serves as a general guide for those working in related fields or those considering the use of EIT. With the above advances, it is a realistic possibility to achieve non-invasive imaging of fast neural activity in real-time with an electrode-atomic magnetometer helmet in human subjects with a resolution of mm and msec.
articles.author: Kai Mason, Kirill Aristovich and David Holder

articles.title: Lower frequency ECoG features improve longitudinal stability of speech and hand-grasp detection in a patient with progressive ALS
articles.content: Objective. Achieving long-term decoding stability is a critical challenge for chronic intracranial brain–computer interfaces (BCIs). High-gamma (HG) activity from intracranial recordings is the standard signal for BCI control, and lower-frequency features can enhance HG decoding performance. This study evaluated the longitudinal stability of speech and hand-grasp detection models using individual and joint spectral features, and the local motor potential (LMP). Approach. Longitudinal data from a single participant implanted with two 64-channel electrocorticographic arrays were used to evaluate the long-term stability of logistic regression models for speech and hand-grasp detection. Models were trained on individual frequency bands and on the LMP, a time-domain low-frequency feature, and evaluated over 21 months for speech and 13 months for grasp. The best-performing band features were then combined into multi-band models and analyzed for their spatial contributions. Main Results. The LMP yielded the most accurate single feature models in both tasks (speech 93.8%, grasp 99.4%) and showed little or no decline. Multi-band models combining HG with lower frequency bands were substantially more stable than HG-only models and outperformed the LMP models for speech but not grasp. HG accuracy degraded strongly for both tasks (speech:−4.3 percentage points per 100 days, or pp/100 d, grasp:−3.4 pp/100 d). HG+beta for speech showed a negligible decline ( 0.5 pp/100 d, 95.6 0.06% overall), and for grasp, delta alone showed remarkable stability (+0.5 pp/100 d), while HG+beta+delta maintained 98.2 0.09% overall accuracy with flat performance (+0.0 pp/100 d). The advantage of the multi-band models increased over time, reaching +20.6 pp for speech and +10.2 pp for grasp in the last 100 days. Significance. Incorporating lower-frequency neural activity yields more stable long-term speech and grasp detection than HG alone. These findings indicate that lower-frequency and multi-band features may reduce recalibration requirements for simple BCI tasks, and may complement the precision control provided by HG activity.
